title: How Architects Solve Common Problems in Older Westchester Homes
excerpt: Older homes throughout Westchester County have charm, but they also have real structural and design challenges. Here's how a licensed architect and general contractor approaches fixing them.
content:
Walk through any neighborhood in Scarsdale, Bronxville, or Larchmont, and you'll see beautiful older homes. Many of them are 50, 75, even 100 years old. They have good bones, character, and land that would cost a fortune to buy today. But they also have problems that their original builders never anticipated.

Outdated electrical systems. Walls that don't line up. Kitchens the size of closets. Bathrooms frozen in time. Floor plans that trap people in separate rooms when everyone wants to gather together. These aren't small issues. They affect how your family actually lives in the house.

The Real Problems Nobody Talks About

When we look at homes in Mamaroneck, Pelham, or Rye, the first thing we check is structural integrity. Old houses often have settling issues. A beam that was fine in 1950 might need reinforcement now. The roof might be sound, but the framing underneath tells a different story. You can't just ignore this and throw new drywall at it.

Then there's the utilities problem. A home built in the 1970s in Eastchester probably has 100-amp electrical service. Today, with air conditioning, home offices, electric vehicle chargers, and multiple devices running constantly, that's not enough. We need to understand what's actually behind your walls before we can design a solution that works.

Flow is another big one. Older homes were built for a different way of living. Separate dining rooms. Closed-off kitchens. Hallways that lead to hallways. Families today want to cook, eat, and gather in one open space. In Harrison or New Rochelle, we're often taking down walls that were load-bearing, which means we need structural support that doesn't exist yet.

How a Design-Build Approach Actually Helps

The reason we work as both an architect and a general contractor isn't just convenient. It's essential when you're solving real problems in older homes. When the architect is also running the construction, there's no gap between what we design and what we can actually build. We see problems while we're drawing, not after framing starts.

Take a second-story addition in Tuckahoe or Ardsley. We need to know exactly how the foundation will handle it. We need to know if the current roof can be removed safely. We need to understand the existing structure well enough to tie new work into it properly. An architect working separate from the contractor might miss these things. By the time they're discovered on site, costs go up and timelines stretch.

When Silvio Luca runs a project, he's personally managing every phase. He's the licensed architect in New York who designed it and the licensed contractor who's building it. That means decisions about problems don't get made in a meeting where nobody's fully accountable. They get made by the person who's responsible for the result.

Working With Local Building Departments

Every town in Westchester has its own building department. Dobbs Ferry, Hastings-on-Hudson, Tarrytown, and Ossining all have permit processes and inspectors. This isn't complicated if you know how to work with them. We do.

Old homes need more scrutiny from inspectors because there's more that can go wrong. A residential architect in Scarsdale or anywhere else in the county needs to understand what those inspectors will actually require. We pull permits that are detailed enough to pass inspection the first time, not permits that generate callbacks and delays.

Home renovations in Westchester County also need to respect local code in ways that newer construction doesn't always require. We know what those codes are and we design around them from the start.

What This Means for Your Home

If you own an older home in any part of Westchester, whether it's a custom home or something you inherited, those structural and design problems are fixable. You don't have to live with them. But they do need to be solved by someone who understands both the architecture and the construction side of the work.
